hints: Picture the alpha-glucose ring you know well with $C_1$ to $C_6$ labelled, then look carefully at $C_1$ and $C_4$ in Fig. 3.1 to see which groups point up and which point down.
walkthrough:
Recall What An Isomer Means**
Galactose has the same molecular formula $C_6H_{12}O_6$ as alpha-glucose, so the atoms are the same and only their arrangement in space is different. That tells you to look for swapped up and down groups, not missing atoms.

Compare C1 and C4**
In alpha-glucose the OH on C1 points down and the OH on C4 points down. In Fig. 3.1 the OH on C1 points up and the OH on C4 points up, with the H atoms in the opposite positions. So both C1 and C4 have H and OH the other way round.
Final answer: At both C1 and C4 the positions of H and OH are reversed compared to alpha-glucose.

hints: Start by sorting the four named sugars in Table 3.1 into the groups you know from the syllabus - which are single-unit monosaccharides and which is the two-unit disaccharide.
Now recall the Benedict's test groups - which of fructose, galactose, glucose and sucrose is the one non-reducing sugar that would need hydrolysis first.
Look down each column in Table 3.1 and across varieties A to E to see if the rank order from highest to lowest sugar is kept the same in every row.
walkthrough:
Sort The Sugars Into Reducing Groups**
Fructose, galactose and glucose are all reducing sugars, while sucrose is non-reducing. Table 3.1 shows a measured value above zero for sucrose in every variety A to E, for example $73.73$ to $89.57$ $mg g^{-1}$ of dry weight, plus large values for fructose and glucose. That proves both reducing and non-reducing sugars are present.

Sort The Sugars Into Size Groups**
Fructose, galactose and glucose each have one ring and are monosaccharides. Sucrose has two rings joined together and is a disaccharide. Because Table 3.1 lists all four sugars in every carrot variety, both monosaccharides and a disaccharide are present.

Check The Pattern Across Varieties**
In every row, fructose is highest at about $157$ to $200$ $mg g^{-1}$, glucose is next at about $125$ to $188$ $mg g^{-1}$, sucrose is next at about $46$ to $90$ $mg g^{-1}$, and galactose is lowest at only $1.13$ to $5.99$ $mg g^{-1}$. The actual numbers change but the rank order fructose > glucose > sucrose > galactose is identical, so the pattern is the same.

Final answer: Conclusion 1: fructose, galactose and glucose are reducing sugars and sucrose is a non-reducing sugar, so both types are present. Conclusion 2: fructose, galactose and glucose are monosaccharides and sucrose is a disaccharide, so both types are present. Conclusion 3: all varieties show the same order of content: fructose highest, then glucose, then sucrose, then galactose lowest.

hints: Think beyond sweet soluble sugars to the large insoluble carbohydrate polymers that build plant cells or store energy in a root.
walkthrough:
Think Polymer Not Monomer**
Sugars like glucose and sucrose are small and soluble and taste sweet. Carrot roots also need long-chain polysaccharides for support in cell walls and for storage. Any one example such as starch for storage, or cellulose, hemicellulose and pectin for cell walls, is a carbohydrate that is not a sugar.
Final answer: Starch (or cellulose / hemicellulose / pectin / amylose / amylopectin / inulin).

hints: Follow the age of the plant - when is the thick carrot root filling up with sugars made in the leaves, and when is it emptying to feed new growth.
Remember what a source does in phloem transport - it is the place where sugars like sucrose are loaded into phloem for export to growing parts.
Remember what a sink does - it is the place that receives and uses or stores imported sugars, such as a growing root or a developing shoot.
walkthrough:
Sink In Year One**
In the first year leaves photosynthesise and make sucrose. The young carrot root is growing and cannot meet its own needs, so it imports assimilates in phloem sap and converts them for storage, e.g. into starch. A region that receives and stores assimilates is a sink.

Source In Year Two**
After the dormant period the plant uses the carrot as a food reserve. Stored starch is broken down to soluble sugars which are loaded into phloem and translocated out of the carrot to developing shoots, buds, flowers and seeds. A region that exports assimilates is a source, so the carrot is now only a source.

Link Structure To Function**
Source means the start of translocation, providing sugars for growth elsewhere. Sink means the arrival point, using sugars for respiration, growth or building a store. The same organ swaps roles because the direction of need reverses between building the store in year one and spending the store in year two.

Final answer: Sink in first year of growth when assimilates are transported to the carrot for growth and storage. Source in second year after dormancy when stored assimilates are mobilised, e.g. starch to sugars, and loaded into phloem for transport to growing shoots, flowers and seeds.

hints: Look at Fig. 3.2 and note the type of nucleic acid packaged inside the capsid - how does that compare with the DNA normally found in a plant cell nucleus.
Recall the normal flow from DNA to RNA to protein and ask which step can be skipped if the incoming viral genome already has the same base sequence as messenger RNA.
walkthrough:
Why No Transcription**
Normal plant cells transcribe DNA into mRNA in the nucleus. Fig. 3.2 shows this potyvirus carries RNA inside its capsid and has no DNA. With no viral DNA present there is nothing to transcribe, so transcription cannot happen.

Why Translation Can Happen Directly**
The viral RNA already has the codon sequence of mRNA. Host ribosomes in the carrot cell cytoplasm can bind to it and translate it straight away, joining amino acids together to build viral capsid and other viral proteins.
Final answer: Viral genetic material is RNA not DNA, so transcription does not occur. Viral RNA acts as mRNA and can be translated directly by host ribosomes to make viral proteins / polypeptides.
